text_blocks.snippet: [Highlight start] Metal roofing (such as standing seam or stone-coated steel) and Class IV impact-rated architectural shingles (especially SBS-modified) [Highlight end] are generally the best roofing materials for Utah's mix of heavy snow, strong winds, hail, and high-elevation UV exposure.
snippet_highlighted_words: [Highlight start] Metal roofing (such as standing seam or stone-coated steel) and Class IV impact-rated architectural shingles (especially SBS-modified) [Highlight end]

list.snippet: Standing Seam & Metal Panels: Shed snow easily to help prevent ice dams, resist intense UV at higher elevations, and typically last 40–60+ years. Look for heavier gauges (such as 24-gauge minimum) and snow guards where heavy snow slides off.

Stone-Coated Steel: Combines metal durability with shingle or tile aesthetics, strong wind and Class 4 impact ratings, and a 50+ year lifespan with a higher upfront cost. See CK Builders for details on stone-coated steel and low-slope membranes in Utah.

Class IV Impact-Rated (SBS-Modified) Asphalt Shingles: A more budget-friendly option that adds rubber-like flexibility and better UV/hail/wind resistance than standard asphalt shingles. Learn more about impact-rated shingles in Elevated Roofing and Siding .

Clay, Concrete Tile, or Natural Slate: Last 50–100+ years and handle heat well, though they are heavy and require roof framing that can support the load. For local climate trade-offs across metal, tile, and slate, see Legacy Roofing .
